The TD error

The bracket in Lesson 45's update has a name: the TD error, $\delta$. It is surprise: how much better or worse things just turned out than the agent expected. Dopamine neurons in the brain fire in a pattern that closely matches it.

Each trial lasts 20 time steps. A light comes on at step 4 (blue) and juice arrives 8 steps later, at step 12 (amber). The agent learns a value for each step since the light with TD(0). Bars show $\delta$ at each step of the latest trial.

$V$ at each step after the latest trial (darker green = higher):

Every trial so far, newest at the bottom (green $\delta > 0$, red $\delta < 0$):

Train for 30 or so trials, then tick "withhold the juice" and run one more.

The maths

The TD error at step $t$ compares the old estimate with the one-step target:

$$\delta_t = R_{t+1} + \gamma V(S_{t+1}) - V(S_t)$$

Positive means things went better than expected; negative means worse. TD(0) is then $V(S_t) \leftarrow V(S_t) + \alpha\,\delta_t$.

If $V$ does not change during an episode, the Monte Carlo error is the discounted sum of the TD errors (S&B eq. 6.6). Add and subtract $\gamma V(S_{t+1})$:

$$\begin{aligned} G_t - V(S_t) &= R_{t+1} + \gamma G_{t+1} - V(S_t) + \gamma V(S_{t+1}) - \gamma V(S_{t+1}) \\ &= \delta_t + \gamma\big(G_{t+1} - V(S_{t+1})\big) \\ &= \delta_t + \gamma \delta_{t+1} + \gamma^2\big(G_{t+2} - V(S_{t+2})\big) \\ &= \sum_{k=t}^{T-1} \gamma^{k-t} \delta_k \end{aligned}$$

The last line uses $G_T - V(S_T) = 0 - 0$ at the terminal state. Monte Carlo waits for the whole sum; TD uses each term as it arrives.

In the trial, the steps before the light share one value, held at $0$: in experiments the light comes at unpredictable times, so nothing before it predicts juice. With $\gamma = 1$ and the values learned, every step from the light until the juice is worth $1$ and later steps are worth $0$. So:

$$\delta_{\text{light}} = 0 + 1 - 0 = 1, \qquad \delta_{\text{juice}} = 1 + 0 - 1 = 0, \qquad \delta_{\text{no juice}} = 0 + 0 - 1 = -1$$

The surprise moves to the earliest reliable predictor of reward, and a missing reward produces a dip.

Schultz, Dayan and Montague (1997) showed that midbrain dopamine neurons in monkeys do the same three things: they fire for unexpected juice, shift their firing to a cue that predicts the juice, and pause when predicted juice does not arrive. The tabular model also predicts that the burst creeps backwards step by step during learning; whether real neurons show that gradual shift has been debated for years.
